intro: The Budget is out. Three audiences read it, and each says why.

reading.label: Change in spending on departments in the target year

rules.note: Departments only: benefits have rules of their own. About a fifth of March’s £23.6bn headroom either way is felt; fifteen billion of cuts is a programme of them.
rules.nudge: {gap} more for public services would have lifted the backbenchers’ rating.

bands.text: Departments lose {abs} a year against their plans. The benches did not come into politics for cuts this deep.
Public services lose {abs} against the Spending Review. A minister will name the service that pays.
Public spending is about where the Spending Review left it ({value}).

variants.text: Spending on departments nets out near the plan ({value}), with cuts to {cutServices}.

bands.text: Public services get {abs} more than the Spending Review planned. That is what the party came in to do.

variants.text: Public services get {abs} more in all, but with cuts to {cutServices}.

reading.label: Welfare decisions of Budget 2025 reversed

rules.note: Any reversal counts; the two-child limit, the PIP changes and winter fuel were the three fights of last November.

bands.text: Last November’s welfare U-turns stand. Ending the two-child limit was scored as lifting 450,000 children out of poverty.
A welfare cut the party fought to reverse is back. Last year’s argument now runs backwards.
More than one of last November’s welfare U-turns is undone. The left of the party will fight again.

reading.label: Change in benefits in the target year

rules.note: Two billion a year either way is felt in benefit rates; five billion of cuts is a programme of them. Smaller moves are absorbed in uprating.
rules.nudge: {gap} more on benefits would have lifted the backbenchers’ rating.

bands.text: Benefits are cut by {abs} a year. The benches will fight a programme of cuts this size.
Benefits are cut by {abs} a year. The benches will ask who this falls on.
Benefit spending is about where the forecast had it ({value}).
Benefits rise by {abs} a year. The benches will be glad to defend that.

reading.label: Revenue from the top and business, less revenue from everyone else

rules.note: The balance of new revenue: the best-off, savers and business on one side; everyone who earns or spends, motorists and duties on the other. Two billion either way is the threshold.
rules.nudge: {gap} more from the best-off and business, rather than the broad base, would have lifted the backbenchers’ rating.

bands.text: The new money comes mainly from {payers}, not the top: {abs} net. The benches remember the manifesto.
What is raised is spread between the broad base and the top ({value} net).
More is asked of {payers} than of everyone else: {abs} net. The benches wanted this.

reading.label: Manifesto red lines crossed

rules.note: The tax lock, the corporation tax cap and the triple lock: the 2024 manifesto’s own words. A decision of last year’s Budget reversed is a U-turn, with rules of its own.

bands.text: Every manifesto red line holds. MPs in marginal seats have nothing to explain on the doorstep.
A manifesto red line is crossed, and the words are on the record. Marginal-seat MPs will be asked first.

reading.label: Manifesto promises strained

rules.note: The levy, the employer-side National Insurance charges and a new top rate keep the pledge’s words and test its spirit: the government’s own reading in October 2024, contested then and now. Amber, not red: one point, and no floor.

bands.text: Nothing here tests the pledge’s spirit while keeping its words.
A tax rise that keeps the letter of the manifesto and not its spirit. The benches will argue about it.

reading.label: Flagships agreed with the Prime Minister no longer funded

rules.note: Any priority agreed in Downing Street with nothing behind it. A priority only started is said in words and scores nothing (Phase 25).

bands.text: Everything agreed in Downing Street has something behind it in the Budget.

variants.text: Every priority has something behind it, but some only make a start. No. 10 will ask for more.

bands.text: A priority agreed in Downing Street has nothing behind it. No. 10 will notice before anyone else.

reading.label: Fiscal rules missed: the day-to-day rule and the debt rule

rules.note: The Chancellor told the Treasury Committee the government will abide by the fiscal rules. A miss costs a point, and holds the benches at three whatever else the Budget does.

bands.text: Both fiscal rules are met, as the Chancellor told the Treasury Committee they would be.
A fiscal rule is missed. The Chancellor promised the Treasury Committee to abide by them; the benches will be asked to defend it.

audiences.title: The markets
audiences.question: Is the headroom enough? What about growth and the tax burden?

reading.label: Headroom against the day-to-day rule

rules.note: Ten billion is where commentators called the margin wafer-thin before the last Budget doubled it to £21.7bn; twenty is your advisers’ rule of thumb. Above about twenty-seven billion the margin is more than March left. The fall from March’s £23.6bn to today’s estimate came before any measure: dearer borrowing and prices since March.
rules.nudge: {gap} more headroom would have lifted the markets’ rating.

bands.text: The day-to-day rule is missed by {abs}, and the OBR will say so on Budget day. Gilt investors read that first.
Headroom of {abs} is below the ten billion commentators called wafer-thin before the last Budget. Thin margins are noticed.

variants.text: Headroom of {abs} is below the ten billion commentators called wafer-thin. Dearer borrowing and prices since March took it, not your measures.

bands.text: Headroom of {abs}: less than March left, and smaller than the OBR’s typical forecast error of about {typicalError}.
Headroom of {abs}, above the twenty billion your advisers call comfortable and close to what March left. A buffer, as promised.
Headroom of {abs}, more than the £23.6bn March left. A wide buffer: money raised that this Budget does not spend.

reading.label: Change in borrowing in the target year, from before your Budget

rules.note: Five billion less is a change in the financing remit the market notices; ten billion more is an issuance programme it prices.
rules.nudge: {gap} less borrowing in the target year would have lifted the markets’ rating.

bands.text: Borrowing in the target year is {abs} lower than before your Budget: fewer gilts to sell into a nervous market.
Borrowing is close to where it was before your Budget ({value}). Yields at about 5.3% against the OBR’s 4.5% matter more.
Borrowing is {abs} higher than before your Budget: more gilts to sell where yields were already about 5.3% against 4.5%.

reading.label: Change in the tax take as a share of the economy, from before your Budget

rules.note: Half a point of GDP on top of a tax take the OBR already calls a historic high.
rules.nudge: {gap} less on the tax take would have lifted the markets’ rating.

bands.text: The tax take moves by {abs} of the economy. The forecast already has it at 38.5% of GDP by 2030-31, a historic high.
The tax take rises by {abs} of the economy. That is on top of 38.5% of GDP by 2030-31, already a historic high.

reading.label: Cuts to departments’ day-to-day budgets, counted one by one

rules.note: Ten billion a year of cuts against plans, on top of the squeeze the forecast already assumes: it has unprotected day-to-day spending falling 4.4% a year in real terms in its last two years.
rules.nudge: {gap} less in cuts to departments would have lifted the markets’ rating.

bands.text: No department’s day-to-day budget is cut against its plan.
Departments lose {abs} against their plans: not enough for the markets to doubt it.
Departments lose {abs} against their plans, on top of the squeeze the forecast already assumes. Cuts this deep are hard to hold.

sources.quote: falling by 4.4 per cent a year in real terms in the final two years of the forecast

reading.label: Change in public investment in the target year

rules.note: A cut of more than about two billion a year to capital budgets.

bands.text: Public investment is cut by {abs}. The 2024 rules were written so it would not be the first thing cut.
Public investment: {value} against the plan. It counts against the debt rule, not the day-to-day rule.

reading.label: Headroom against the debt rule

rules.note: Net financial liabilities falling as a share of GDP in the target year, or not. A miss is treated like a miss of the day-to-day rule.

bands.text: The debt rule is missed by {abs}: debt no longer falls as a share of the economy. Gilt investors watch the debt path.
Debt still falls as a share of the economy: the debt rule is met.

reading.label: Share of the improvement resting on uncertified costings

rules.note: Two-fifths of the yield: beyond that the OBR’s own scoring, not the Budget, sets the number.

bands.text: What improves the current budget rests mostly on HMRC rows and Treasury lines the OBR will certify.
More than two-fifths of the yield rests on figures nobody has certified. The OBR may score them lower.

variants.text: More than two-fifths of the yield is what tax breaks cost today. HMRC says ending them raises less.

reading.label: Whether what the Budget spends and gives away is paid for in every year

rules.note: Paid for: measures that cost something, with borrowing no higher than before the Budget in any year. The Resolution Foundation said new commitments must be fully funded from the start.

bands.text: Everything new is paid for in every year, as the Resolution Foundation said new commitments must be.

sources.quote: Any new spending commitments must be fully funded from the start.

bands.text: Nothing here needed paying for.
Some of what the Budget spends or gives away is borrowed, in at least one year.

reading.label: Borrowing in an earlier year above what the target year shows

rules.note: The rules test one year. Five billion a year more borrowing in an earlier year than the target year shows is issuance the market funds all the same.

bands.text: No earlier year borrows much more than the target year shows.
Borrowing is {abs} higher in an earlier year than the target year shows. The rules test one year; the market funds them all.

reading.label: Share of the new tax money in the target year that raises nothing in the first year

rules.note: A quarter of the new tax money: beyond that, much of what the rules count has yet to be collected when the markets judge the Budget. The line is the game’s, and it moves no rating.

bands.text: No new tax money waits until {lateFrom} or later to arrive.
{value} of the new tax money in {year} waits until {lateFrom} or later. Most of it arrives from the start.
{value} of the new tax money in {year} waits until {lateFrom} or later. The markets will want to see it arrive.

audiences.title: The public
audiences.question: Did it make a difference to them?

reading.label: Manifesto promises broken

rules.note: One is enough. Crossing a manifesto red line, the 2024 manifesto’s own words, pins the rating at the floor whatever else the Budget does.

bands.text: Every manifesto red line holds.
A manifesto promise has been broken. The pledge was made on every doorstep, and nothing else will be heard.

reading.label: Manifesto promises strained

rules.note: A promise kept in the words and tested in the spirit costs a point, never the floor: the floor is for the pledge’s own words.

bands.text: Nothing here tests the pledge’s spirit while keeping its words.
A promise kept in the words and tested in the spirit. People notice a National Insurance rise by another name.

reading.label: Decisions of last year’s Budget reversed, outside the manifesto

rules.note: Bringing back what last year’s Budget ended, such as the two-child limit: a U-turn, not a manifesto red line. One point, and no floor.

bands.text: Last year’s Budget decisions stand.
You reversed a decision from last year’s Budget. It was not a manifesto promise, but people notice a U-turn.

reading.label: Fiscal rules missed: the day-to-day rule and the debt rule

rules.note: The government promised to meet its fiscal rules. A miss costs a point and holds the public at three, whatever else the Budget does. The welfare cap is not counted here.

bands.text: The government promised to meet its fiscal rules, and on these numbers it does.
The government promised to meet its fiscal rules. On these numbers it does not.

reading.label: Priorities delivered in full

rules.note: A priority counts when a way to deliver it in full is on. A start or a trimmed ask is said in words and scores nothing (Phase 25).

bands.text: No priority was delivered in full: nothing people can point at yet.

variants.text: Your priorities are started, not delivered. People notice a start far less than a result.

bands.text: One of the Budget’s priorities is delivered in full. People will notice it.

variants.text: One priority is delivered in full; the others only make a start. People will notice the one.

bands.text: Two or more of the Budget’s priorities are delivered in full. People can see what it was for.

reading.label: Money behind a single, fully delivered priority

rules.note: One priority ranked, delivered, and at least five billion a year behind it: a Budget people can describe in a sentence.
rules.nudge: {gap} more behind a single priority would have made it a story people can describe.

bands.text: There is no single story: more than one priority, an option cut back, or too little money behind it.
One clear priority with {abs} a year behind it: a Budget people can describe in a sentence.

reading.label: Cuts to departments’ day-to-day budgets, counted one by one

rules.note: Three billion a year of cuts against plans is noticed and ten is felt widely; cuts to health and schools are noticed from two billion. A cut is counted even when another budget rises.

bands.text: No public service gets noticeably less than planned.

variants.text: Every public service gets at least what was planned.

bands.text: Public services get {abs} less than planned. People notice cuts in the services they use.

variants.text: Cuts to {protected}: {protectedCut} a year less than planned. These are the services people use most.

bands.text: Public services get {abs} less than planned, and people will notice.

variants.text: Cuts to {protected}: {protectedCut} a year less than planned, and {abs} across services in all. People will notice.

reading.label: Tax rises most households feel, in the target year

rules.note: Five billion a year passes quietly; twenty is felt by most households before the target year. Levies on banks, energy producers and the very top are left out: most households do not feel them.
rules.nudge: {gap} less in tax rises would have lifted the public’s rating.

bands.text: Tax rises of {abs} a year, felt {feltHow}: small enough to pass without a fight.

variants.text: No tax rise most households will feel.

bands.text: Tax rises of {abs} a year, felt {feltHow}, well before the target year.
Tax rises of {abs} a year, felt {feltHow}, on top of a tax take already at a historic high.

reading.label: Tax rises on banks, energy producers and the very top

rules.note: No point either way: most households do not feel these, and the game has no published measure of how the public sees them.

bands.text: Nothing here falls only on banks, energy producers or the very top.
{abs} a year falls on banks, energy producers or the very top: most households will not feel it.

reading.label: Tax cuts in the target year

rules.note: A billion a year is the least a cut can be and still be noticed.

bands.text: No tax cut to speak of.
Tax cuts worth {abs} a year, with the cost of living back at the centre of politics.

sources.quote: the cost-of-living crisis is back centre stage
